answers: Chart of accounts, counterparties (own company, customers, suppliers), catalogue items, warehouse locations, and VAT rates are each separate master-data objects; counterparties also store an IBAN where known.

So what we've got for master data is this: the chart of accounts gets its own object, then all the companies we work with — that's ourselves, our customers, and our suppliers — each get their own object too, and same goes for catalogue items, warehouse locations, and VAT rates; oh, and whenever we've got a bank account number for a company, we store that IBAN right on their record.

Each of the following lives as its own master-data object: the chart of accounts, every company we deal with (our own company, customers, and suppliers), catalogue items, warehouse locations, and VAT rates — and any company record can also hold that company's IBAN if we've got it.

Sales invoices we issue are recorded as sales_invoice documents. Each one captures: number, issue date, seller and buyer (looked up by NIP), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + payment days from the invoice; status begins as open, later moving to paid. Open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched; partly paid invoices stay open, and a paid invoice reverts to open if its match is undone. Posting is in book pl-stat: debit 201 for gross, credit 700 for net, credit 222 for VAT.

So whenever we send out a sales invoice, the system creates a document of type sales_invoice, and it pulls in the number, the issue date, the seller and the buyer — both found using NIP — plus the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code straight off the invoice. To work out VAT you take the net, multiply by the rate's percentage, divide by 100, and round half up to the grosz, then gross is just net plus that VAT figure. The due date is calculated by adding however many payment days are printed on the invoice to the issue date. Status-wise it kicks off as open and can flip to paid down the line. The open amount starts out equal to the gross and ticks down every time a payment gets matched against it; if it's only partly paid it stays open, and if it was fully paid but the match gets undone, it flips back to open again. For the bookkeeping entry in book pl-stat, you debit account 201 with the gross, credit account 700 with the net, and credit account 222 with the VAT.

Each outgoing sales invoice gets logged as a sales_invoice doc — grabs the number, issue date, seller & buyer by NIP, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT calc: net × rate% / 100, half-up rounding to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + invoice's payment days; status opens as open, can go to paid. Open amount kicks off at gross, drops as payments match; partly paid stays open, paid flips back to open if the match is undone. Book pl-stat entry: debit 201 gross, credit 700 net, credit 222 VAT.

Each delivery produces exactly one PZ document — type pz — carrying the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency. Each item on that delivery becomes a pz_line tied to the PZ, holding qty, price, and value, where value equals qty times the unit price from the delivery. Every pz_line moves the item's stock into the location on the PZ and posts to ledger pl-stat: debit 330, credit 300, at that line's value.

So for every single delivery that comes in, you're going to create one PZ document — that's the goods received note, and the type is literally called pz — and on that document you need the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency, all of those. Then for each item that was delivered, you create a separate line under that PZ, and the type for those lines is pz_line, and each one links back to its parent PZ and has three fields on it: qty, price, and value, and the value is just the quantity multiplied by the unit price that's written on the delivery. And every one of those lines has to move that item's stock into whichever location is on the delivery, and it also needs to post a booking in the book pl-stat — debit goes to 330 and credit goes to 300 — and the amount posted is the value on that line.

One delivery, one PZ — that's your goods received note, type pz — with the supplier, their delivery doc number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency on it. Every item gets its own pz_line hanging off that PZ, with qty, price, and value on it; value is just qty times the unit price off the delivery. Each of those lines bumps the item's stock into the delivery's location and throws a posting into pl-stat: 330 debit, 300 credit, for that line's value.

A supplier invoice gets recorded as a purchase_invoice document with these fields: number, invoice date, supplier looked up by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the nearest grosz; gross = net + VAT. Status begins as open and moves to paid when matched; a partial match leaves it open. The open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched; undoing a match flips a paid invoice back to open. Posting goes into book pl-stat: debit 300 for net, debit 221 for VAT, credit 202 for gross.

So when a supplier sends us an invoice, what we do is create a document of type purchase_invoice, and we fill in the number, the invoice date, the supplier — we find them using their NIP — then our own company goes in as the owner, and we record the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. Now, to work out the VAT, you take the net, multiply it by the rate's percentage, divide by 100, and round that result half up to the grosz — that's your VAT amount — and then gross is simply net plus VAT. The status on a brand-new invoice is always open, and it only moves to paid once payments have been matched against it; if a payment only covers part of it, the invoice stays open. The open amount starts life equal to the gross and comes down as each payment is matched; and if you ever undo a match on something that had reached paid, it flips right back to open again. For the accounting side, every purchase invoice gets posted in the pl-stat book: you debit account 300 with the net, debit account 221 with the VAT, and credit account 202 with the gross.

Supplier invoice comes in — bang, you make a purchase_invoice, slap on the number, invoice date, supplier by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, VAT rate code. VAT's just net times the rate percent over 100, round half up to the grosz, gross is net plus that VAT. Starts open, goes paid when matched, stays open if it's only partly matched, and if you undo a match on a paid one it pops back to open. Open amount kicks off at gross and drops as payments hit it. Book pl-stat: debit 300 with net, debit 221 with VAT, credit 202 with gross.
Each warehouse goods issue creates a goods_issue document with fields item, location, quantity, date, and reason, and reduces that item's stock at that location.

So when stuff goes out of the warehouse, the system logs it as a goods_issue — you've got your item, location, quantity, date, and reason on there — and that pulls the stock for that item right out of its location.

A goods_issue document, carrying the item, location, quantity, date, and reason fields, is produced whenever goods leave the warehouse, and the stock of that item is removed from the relevant location as a result of every such issue.

Each bank statement line is stored as a bank_line record with date, amount, currency, direction, reference (the title), counterparty name and account, and our account; open amount is initialised to the amount, status to open, flipping to settled once open amount hits zero. Incoming money is applied to the customer's open sales invoices: first the invoice named in the title; then that same invoice if the gap is within 0.02, with the difference written off to 755; then an invoice for exactly that amount; then the fewest invoices summing to it, up to 4; then the named invoice partially; otherwise the oldest open invoices in sequence until the money runs out. Outgoing money follows the same steps against the supplier's open purchase invoices, but without the 0.02 tolerance. Each match reduces the open amounts on both the invoices and the bank line by the allocated figure, marks them paid or settled when fully cleared, and writes a settlement record holding the payment, document type and id, amount, and date. A tolerated difference produces a matching difference record with kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date, and if it is short it is booked in pl-stat as a debit to the difference account and a credit to 201. Anything left unmatched is displayed as open lines alongside open invoices for manual pairing.

So here's the deal: every single line on the bank statement gets its own bank_line record — you've got the date on there, the amount, the currency, which direction the money's going, the title from the statement as the reference field, who the counterparty is plus their account number, and then our account too; the open amount kicks off equal to the full amount, status starts as open, and it only flips to settled once there's nothing left open on it. Now, when money comes in, you're matching it against the open sales invoices belonging to whatever customer that account number points to, and you work through the steps in order: first up, if the title literally names an invoice, you go with that one; next, if that named invoice is within 0.02 — either short or over — you still match it but you write the difference off to account 755; after that, you look for any invoice that's the exact same amount; then you try to find the smallest group of invoices — four at the most — that add up to it; if that doesn't work you partially match the named invoice; and if none of that flies you just start eating through the oldest open invoices until the money's gone. Money going out works exactly the same way but it's against the supplier's open purchase invoices for whichever account it's heading to, and you skip the 0.02 tolerance bit entirely. Whenever you get a match, the open amounts on both the invoice side and the bank line side drop by whatever got allocated, they get flagged paid or settled when they're fully cleared, and you log a settlement record for each invoice that captures the payment, the document type and id, the amount, and the date. If there's a tolerated difference you create a matching difference record covering the kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date, and when that difference is short you post it in pl-stat: debit goes to the difference account, credit goes to 201. Whatever nothing managed to settle gets shown side by side — open lines on one side, open invoices on the other — so a human can go in and pair them up manually.

Bank statement line → bank_line; fields: date, amount, currency, direction, title as reference, counterparty plus their account, our account; open amount = amount at creation; status = open, becomes settled at zero open amount. Inbound cash: match against the named customer's open sales invoices — step 1, the invoice the title specifies; step 2, that invoice where the shortfall or excess is at most 0.02, difference to 755; step 3, any invoice for exactly that amount; step 4, the fewest invoices totalling it, maximum 4; step 5, partial match on the named invoice; step 6, oldest open invoices until funds exhausted. Outbound cash: same sequence against the named supplier's open purchase invoices, tolerance step omitted. On each match: open amounts on the invoice(s) and the line decrease by the allocated amount, status becomes paid or settled when fully cleared, and a settlement record is written — payment, document type and id, amount, date — per invoice. Tolerated difference → matching difference record: kind, amount, currency, direction, account, date; if short, post in pl-stat, debit difference account, credit 201. Unresolved items: open lines and open invoices displayed side by side for manual pairing.

Complaints get logged as complaint docs with a number, customer, and details. Each one spawns a case-type record where the subject is that complaint number and the status kicks off as open, then can shift to resolved.

So when a customer complaint comes in, you record it as a complaint document — it carries a number, the customer, and the details. That complaint document then automatically triggers the creation of a follow-up item: the type on that item is called case, its subject field holds the complaint number, and its status begins at open, with the possibility of moving over to resolved down the line.

Each customer complaint goes in as a complaint document — number, customer, details — and every single one of those kicks off a follow-up record typed as case, with the subject set to the complaint number and the status starting at open, moving to resolved later.
A withdrawn complaint gets its case marked resolved.
So basically, if the customer decides to pull back their complaint, what happens is that the case tied to it ends up being resolved — that's how it works.
Pull the complaint, the case closes out as resolved.

A stock count at a location creates a stock_level record with four fields: date, counted, book, and difference. Book is the sum of inbound stock movements minus outbound ones for that item and location up to and including the count date. Difference is counted minus book.

So when you do a stock count for an item at a location, what you're recording is a new type called stock_level, and it's got four fields on it — date, which is the count date, then counted, which is how many you physically counted, then book, which you work out by taking all that item's stock movements into the location and subtracting all the ones going out, but only including movements dated up to and including the count date, and finally difference, which is just counted minus book.

For a stock count of an item at a location, you're storing a stock_level — that's the type name — and it carries the count date as date, the physically counted quantity as counted, the book quantity as book, where book means all that item's stock movements into the location minus all those out of it with dates up to and including the count date, and then difference, which is counted minus book.
